passage: In Santiago, Pablo stood in the hallway with his running shoes in his hand and thought about quitting. Six weeks of training, and his legs felt heavy and his times were worse. He phoned Nour, who coached the university running group. "Is it the race, the plan, or just a rough patch?" she asked. He thought about it. He still wanted the race. The plan was three hard runs a week with no rest, and his semester exams were this week. So he cut it to two easy runs, swapped one for a bike ride and wrote "review on the 20th" on the fridge whiteboard. On the 20th his legs felt lighter, and he chose to keep going.

qa.q: What did Pablo write on the fridge whiteboard?
qa.a: Pablo wrote "review on the 20th".

qa.q: How did Pablo feel once he thought about Nour's question?
qa.a: Pablo felt steadier and still determined, because he realised he still wanted the race, so the goal itself was not the problem.

qa.q: Why was the review date a useful step?
qa.a: It turned quitting into a considered choice, letting him try a lighter plan before deciding.

qa.q: How might Nour have felt about Pablo's call?
qa.a: Glad to help, and probably pleased that Pablo was checking the goal, the plan and the phase before quitting.

grounding: Illustrates a person who asks whether the goal, the method or a passing phase is the problem, adjusts the plan and sets a review date.

passage: In the college music room, Sachin put his guitar back in its case and said, "I think I should quit the band." Preeti, the band's secretary, kept writing in her register. "Is it the music, or the schedule?" "Rehearsal is at eight in the evening and my lab reports are due," Sachin said slowly. "It is the timing. And the fest month is a mess." Preeti suggested moving his slot to Sundays and taking the next two weeks off. They wrote the 14th on the notice board: "Sachin: review." Two weeks later, Sachin walked in with a new riff he had made on the train.

qa.q: What date was written on the notice board for Sachin's review?
qa.a: The 14th was written on the notice board.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling about the band when he said he should quit?
qa.a: Overwhelmed by the schedule pressure and not tired of the music itself.

qa.q: What options did Preeti offer instead of quitting?
qa.a: Moving his slot to Sundays, taking two weeks off and setting a review date.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about a member leaving in the middle of the fest month?
qa.a: Concerned but supportive, since she asked about the cause before accepting the quit.

grounding: Illustrates a person who checks whether a schedule, not the activity, is the problem and pauses with a review date before quitting.

passage:
Dear Ankita,
You asked if I'm still quitting Carnatic singing. I've changed my mind, sort of.
I was ready to stop. I'd been dreading every class for two months. But before I told my guru, I did what you suggested and asked three questions.
Is it the goal? No. I still want to sing. When I hear a good concert, I ache.
Is it the method? Partly. My classes are at 6 a.m., after a late college day. I'm exhausted and my voice isn't awake.
Is it a phase? Also partly. Exams are in three weeks, and everything feels like too much.
So instead of quitting, I asked to move to the Saturday evening batch, and I'm taking two weeks off during exams. I've written a date in my diary: 15 April. On that day I'll ask myself again, honestly.
If I still dread it then, I'll stop, and it'll be a real decision.
Urmila

qa.q: What date did Urmila write in the diary?
qa.a: 15 April.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel about the classes for the past two months?
qa.a: Urmila felt dread about every class, exhausted by the early timing and the exam pressure.

qa.q: How did Urmila's three questions change the decision?
qa.a: They showed the goal was still alive, while the timing and the exam phase were the real problems, so changing the batch and pausing made more sense than quitting.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ankita would probably feel pleased and a little proud that the suggestion helped Urmila make a considered choice.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who asks whether the problem is the goal, the method or a phase, adjusts and pauses, and sets a review date before quitting.

passage:
Nazia, you asked on the show how I nearly quit running. I'm Sahil, and I trained for a half-marathon last year.
Around week eight, I hated it. I'd wake up at five, drag myself out, and come back angry. I was about to delete the training plan.
My older cousin asked me to sit down first and answer three things. Did I still want to run a half-marathon? Yes, honestly. Was the method wrong? Maybe: I was doing every run alone, in the dark, at the same hard pace. Was it a phase? My college placements were that month, so everything felt heavy.
So I didn't quit. I changed the method. Two runs a week with a running group in the evening, one slow long run on Sundays. I took one full week off during placements.
And I set a review date: end of the month. If I still hated it, I'd stop without guilt.
On review day, I didn't hate it. I finished the race in November, slowly, smiling.

qa.q: Around which week did Sahil hate running?
qa.a: Around week eight.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel after the early morning runs around week eight?
qa.a: Sahil felt worn down and angry, coming back from runs ready to delete the plan.

qa.q: What changes did Sahil make instead of quitting?
qa.a: Sahil ran with a group in the evenings, kept one slow long run, took a week off during placements and set a review date.

qa.q: What might Sahil's cousin have felt when Sahil finished the race?
qa.a: The cousin would probably feel proud and pleased that the three questions helped Sahil find a better way instead of quitting.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who checks whether the problem is goal, method or phase, changes the method, pauses and sets a review date.

passage:
I shared a room with Minakshi during her second attempt at the state services exam, so I saw how she decided.
In January she was falling apart. She studied twelve hours a day and remembered nothing. One night she said, "I'm quitting. I'm clearly not good enough."
But the next morning she sat with a notebook instead of packing up her books. I watched her write three headings: Goal. Method. Phase.
Under Goal she wrote, "Still want this." Under Method: "Too much reading, no practice tests." Under Phase: "Grandfather ill, not sleeping."
She took two weeks to be with her grandfather. When she came back, she switched to shorter study blocks and a weekly mock test. On the calendar above her desk she circled 30 April and wrote "Decide."
I don't know exactly what she felt on 30 April. But I saw her tick the date and keep going.
— Alka

qa.q: What date did Minakshi circle on the calendar?
qa.a: 30 April.

qa.q: How did Alka feel watching Minakshi that January?
qa.a: Alka was worried about Minakshi falling apart, and then quietly impressed by how she worked through the decision.

qa.q: What did Minakshi's three headings help her see?
qa.a: That the goal still mattered, the method needed changing and a family phase was part of the strain, so she paused and adjusted instead of quitting.

qa.q: How was Minakshi feeling the night she said she was quitting?
qa.a: Minakshi felt hopeless and inadequate, saying she was clearly not good enough.

grounding: An observer watches a friend ask whether the problem is the goal, the method or a phase, then adjust, pause and set a review date.

passage:
Monday, 3 June. Anand slammed the German textbook shut in the hostel common room. Four months of classes, and he still froze whenever the teacher asked anything out loud. "I'm done. I'm dropping it," he told Joseph.
Joseph didn't argue. "Before you drop it: is it the goal you don't want, or the way you're learning?"
Friday, 7 June. Anand sat with a notebook and made three columns. Goal: the master's in Aachen, still yes. Method: grammar drills alone every night, no speaking; that was the problem. Phase: exam week, sleeping badly. He decided to join a weekend speaking circle, drop half the drills, and take one week off after exams. On the last page he wrote, "Review: 15 July. If I still hate it, I stop."
Monday, 15 July. Anand ordered coffee in German at the speaking circle and got the right cup. He opened the notebook, read the review line, and wrote: "Continue."

qa.q: What review date did Anand set?
qa.a: 15 July.

qa.q: How was Anand feeling on 3 June?
qa.a: Anand felt frustrated and defeated, still freezing whenever asked to speak after four months, and wanted to drop German.

qa.q: What did Joseph's question help Anand do?
qa.a: It helped Anand separate the goal from the method and the phase, so he changed how he learned and set a review date instead of quitting on a bad day.

qa.q: What would change if Joseph had simply agreed that Anand should drop it?
qa.a: Anand might have given up the master's plan because of a poor method and a hard exam week, not because the goal was wrong.

grounding: Shows a person asking whether the goal, the method or a passing phase is the problem, adjusting and setting a review date before quitting.
